scenarios.context: Two students plan a ten-minute presentation.

speakerA.en: We have to give a ten-minute presentation on renewable energy next week. How should we divide the work?
Sounds fair. I'll do the introduction and the part about solar power, and you can cover wind and hydroelectric energy.
Should we use a lot of text on the slides?
What if I forget what to say?
Good advice. How can we start in an interesting way?
I like that. Let's rehearse on Thursday and time ourselves.

speakerB.en: I suggest that we each take one section, and then we practise the whole thing together.
Fine. Then we'll finish with a joint conclusion and invite questions from the audience.
No, keep it minimal. Use short phrases and clear images, and explain the details orally.
Prepare some brief notes, but don't read them word for word. Eye contact makes you more convincing.
A surprising statistic or a question usually works well, such as "What would happen if the sun stopped shining tomorrow?"
Agreed. We can also ask a friend to listen and give us some honest feedback.

scenarios.context: A student contributes to a university-style seminar discussion.

speakerA.en: In the seminar today, I'd like to build on what Maria said earlier about the role of the government.
I don't entirely disagree with her, but I'd argue that local communities also have an important role to play.
Certainly. In my town, residents organised a recycling project that was more successful than the national campaign.
Sorry, could you repeat the last part? I didn't quite catch it.
I see what you mean. That's a valid objection, although some projects can be expanded.
Funding, clear leadership and the support of the people involved, I'd say.

speakerB.en: Please do. It would be helpful if you could explain how your view differs from hers.
Interesting. Could you give us an example to illustrate that point?
That's a useful example, although it suggests that local solutions don't always work on a larger scale.
Of course. I said that success at a local level doesn't guarantee success nationally.
Let's explore that further. What conditions would be necessary for a local project to succeed nationally?
Excellent. Let's write those on the board and then discuss them in groups.

scenarios.scenario: An English speaking test: part one
scenarios.context: An examiner asks a candidate questions about themselves.

speakerA.en: Good morning. Could you tell me your full name and where you are from?
Do you work or are you a student?
What do you enjoy most about your studies?
Let's talk about your free time. How do you usually relax after a busy day?
Is there a hobby that you would like to take up in the future?
Thank you. Now I'm going to give you a topic, and I'd like you to speak about it for one to two minutes.

speakerB.en: Good morning. My name is Elena Petrova, and I come from a small town near the coast.
I'm a student at the moment. I'm studying computer science, although I'm also preparing to move abroad.
I enjoy solving problems logically, and I like the fact that I can see practical results from what I create.
Normally I go for a walk, or I listen to music. It helps me clear my mind.
Yes, I'd love to learn the guitar, but I've never had enough time to practise regularly.
Certainly. Should I take a few moments to make some notes before I begin?

scenarios.context: An examiner asks a candidate for opinions about education and technology.

speakerA.en: Let's discuss the topic in more depth. Do you think technology has improved the way people learn?
Are there any disadvantages?
How do you think schools will change over the next twenty years?
Some people say that teachers will eventually be replaced by computers. What's your opinion?
Should education be free for everyone?
Finally, what advice would you give to someone who wants to improve their English quickly?

speakerB.en: Generally, yes. Students now have access to a huge amount of information, and they can learn at their own pace.
Certainly. It's easy to get distracted, and some people lose the ability to concentrate for long periods.
I suspect that classrooms will become more flexible, with a mixture of online and face-to-face lessons.
I don't think that will happen, because teachers do much more than present information. They motivate and support students.
Ideally, yes, since education is an investment in society. However, governments must find a sustainable way to pay for it.
I'd advise them to practise speaking every day, even if they make mistakes, and to listen to a wide range of accents.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a lecturer for an extension
scenarios.context: A student explains to a lecturer why she needs more time.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, Dr Evans, do you have a moment? I'd like to ask about the deadline for my assignment.
I've been ill for the last week, and I'm afraid I won't be able to submit the work on Friday.
Yes, I have one from my doctor, and I can send you a copy by email this afternoon.
Thank you so much. Would it be possible to have a little longer if I'm still unwell?
I understand. I'll email you on Wednesday to let you know how I'm getting on.
I will. I appreciate your understanding, and I apologise for the inconvenience.

speakerB.en: Of course. What seems to be the problem?
I'm sorry to hear that. Do you have a medical certificate?
That would be helpful. In that case, I can give you an extension of five days.
We'll see how it goes. Please keep me informed, and don't wait until the last moment to tell me.
Good. In the meantime, make sure that you get plenty of rest.
There's no need to apologise. Just focus on getting better.
